name: Central Dravidian
region: Maharashtra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh in central India
defining_innovation: Kolami, Naiki, Parji, Ollari and Gadaba, small languages of central India grouped by shared sound and grammatical changes.

chapters.title: Languages of the Uplands
chapters.body:
The Central Dravidian languages are spoken by tribal communities in the uplands of central India, usually alongside a dominant Indo-Aryan or Dravidian regional language such as Marathi, Telugu, Odia or Halbi. None has more than a few hundred thousand speakers, and Ollari and Gadaba have only a few thousand. They were little known outside the region until Emeneau and Burrow described them in the mid-20th century.

They matter for reconstruction because they preserve features that the big literary languages lost or changed. Whether they form a real subgroup or a set of neighbours is debated, especially in relation to the South-Central languages.

turning_points.title: Kolami–Naiki and Parji–Gadaba
turning_points.description: Central Dravidian divides into a western pair (Kolami, Naiki) and an eastern group (Parji, Ollari, Gadaba). The dates are rough estimates.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Indo-Aryan and Munda neighbours
turning_points.description: Central Dravidian speakers live alongside Indo-Aryan (Marathi, Halbi, Desia) and Munda speakers and borrow words and grammatical patterns from them. Many communities are now bilingual, and some have shifted to the regional language.

sources.citation: Emeneau, Murray B. 1956. India as a linguistic area. Language 32(1).
